The 2024 sheet is probably not the current rate and the 2026 appendix was not read. Treat PASSPORT revenue as a sensitivity case until the current ODA rate sheet is pulled. HB 96 proposed 2% HCBS increases [S24] and a PASSPORT amendment proposed March 1, 2026 rate increases [S31]; enactment was not confirmed. The meaning of the $5.43 'second tier' rate on the same sheet was not verified, so it is not modeled; if it applies to a share of units, revenue would be lower. A 100-client PASSPORT-only agency cannot start without first holding private-pay or non-relative clients [S8]; this model shows the mature state. Full-census staffing is about 6,240 paid aide hours a month (about 48 aide FTEs at 130 hrs/month) plus 7 salaried staff, roughly 55 FTEs. sections.executive_summary:
Ohio **does** license non-medical home care. Some state-hint material and secondary blogs say it does not, but that is wrong. Under ORC Chapter 3740 and OAC Chapter 3701-60, a business that provides nonmedical home health services must hold an Ohio Department of Health (ODH) nonmedical license. The rules took effect for licensure from **October 1, 2022** [S1][S2]. An individual 'nonagency' provider is excluded only if they care for **no more than two** people who are not immediate family [S1]. Any agency, or any provider above that threshold, needs the license. Providers certified by the Department of Developmental Disabilities (Chapter 5123) are listed by ODH among those that do not need the nonmedical license [S33].

The licensing entry cost is low. The application fee is **$250**, non-refundable, and is paid with the application [S3][S4]. New providers (those not operating on or just before Sept. 30, 2021) must also post a **$20,000 surety bond** from an Ohio-licensed surety [S1][S5]. The license renews for $250; confirm the license term, renewal deadline and processing time with ODH, because those details were not confirmed against the rule text. The statute sets no day limit for issuing the license [S1]. The research found no ODH nonmedical staffing ratio, administrator qualification or insurance minimum (see 'What This Report Does Not Claim'). Operators should confirm these with ODH before relying on that absence. Medicaid-billed services carry separate staffing and training rules, summarized in Section 5.

Money comes from two very different streams.

- **Private pay.** The model prices care at **$33/hour**, the Ohio homemaker figure reported by a secondary source citing Genworth/CareScout 2024 [S22]. The national CareScout medians are $34/hour for a home health aide and $33/hour for a homemaker [S21]. A competing secondary source puts the Ohio average at **$28/hour**, with urban areas at $32–$36 [S23]. Neither Ohio figure was checked against the primary CareScout data.
- **Medicaid waiver personal care.** The ODA rate sheet we retrieved (effective Jan. 1, 2024) lists PASSPORT personal care at **$7.24 per 15 minutes ($28.96/hour)** [S14]. That sheet is probably superseded: OAC 5160-1-06.1, which carries the PASSPORT maximum rates, now shows an effective date of April 17, 2026, and we could not read the 2026 appendix. Treat PASSPORT revenue as a sensitivity case. The Ohio Home Care Waiver HCAS/N attendant rate of $6.39 per unit is a nursing-task rate outside non-medical scope [S13]. Managed care plans are not bound to fee-for-service rates [S16]. ODM also paused new Medicaid enrollment for home health, hospice and related provider types from **May 14 to Nov. 14, 2026** [S28][S29]. Whether personal care aide and home care attendant types are covered was not confirmed. If they are, no Medicaid billing can start before about Nov. 14, 2026.

The default model is a **35-client private-pay agency** with a full-time administrator, one client care supervisor and one scheduler/billing coordinator. At 90% census it nets about **$9,942 a month (12.0% margin)**. It breaks even near **59.6% occupancy**, reaches its first profitable month in **month 9**, and needs about **$89,381** of modeled cash to get there. The same agency priced at $28/hour **loses about $2,469 a month and never breaks even** at 100% census. A PASSPORT-only agency of 100 clients nets just $2,840 a month (1.8%) and needs about $398,450 of cash, and that result rests on a 2024 rate that is probably superseded. The Medicaid configurations also omit some required costs (RN/LPN supervision for Home Care Waiver billing, after-hours supervisor coverage, back-up aide capacity, paid in-service time, overtime, aide mileage and, at 100 clients, possible ACA employer coverage), so their real margins are lower than shown. The honest conclusion is that private-pay price and aide wage control profitability in Ohio, and Medicaid is a later add-on rather than a launch strategy.
sections.service_model:
**Who is served.** Non-medical home care serves older adults and people with disabilities who need help with daily living at home. Examples are bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting and mobility, plus household help such as meals, laundry and light housekeeping. Ohio's statute defines nonmedical home health services to include personal care and assistance managing the individual's home and handling personal affairs [S1]. Medicaid-funded personal care is defined by ODA as hands-on assistance with ADLs, and with IADLs when incidental to providing ADLs, in the individual's home and community [S32].

**What the state calls it.** The ODH license is a 'nonmedical home health services' license under ORC Chapter 3740 and OAC Chapter 3701-60 [S1][S2]. Medicaid pathways sit with separate agencies:

- **ODA PASSPORT personal care.** Certified under OAC 173-39 [S32].
- **ODM Ohio Home Care Waiver and Medicaid personal care aide.** OAC Chapter 5160-46 covers the home care waiver, including the personal care aide rule 5160-46-04 and the attendant rule 5160-46-06.1. OAC 5160-58-04 covers the Medicaid personal care aide service (HCPCS T1019) [S11][S13][S15].

**Scope limits.** A waiver personal care aide may not administer prescribed or over-the-counter medications, only help the client self-administer [S11]. Skilled nursing is outside non-medical licensure. The PASSPORT rate sheet lists waiver nursing separately [S14].

**Business models.** (1) A private-pay agency billing families directly. (2) A mixed agency serving private-pay clients plus PASSPORT or other Medicaid clients. (3) A Medicaid-focused agency. Under participant direction, the individual is the employer and the provider is the employee, which is a different operating model from an agency [ODA participant direction page; see S14 context]. This report models the three agency types.
sections.licensing_pathway:
**Step 1 — Confirm you need the license.** An agency providing nonmedical home health services needs the ODH license beginning Oct. 1, 2022 [S2]. An individual nonagency provider needs it if they care for more than two individuals who are not immediate family [S1]. Check whether any exemption applies, for example DODD-certified providers [S33].

**Step 2 — Form the business.** Create the legal entity and EIN before applying. The Ohio LLC Articles of Organization fee of $99 appears only on secondary sites and should be verified with the Secretary of State.

**Step 3 — Assemble the application.** ORC 3740.03 and OAC 3701-60-03 require, among other items:

- A statement of the **days and hours of operation** [S1].
- A **fingerprint impression card** from the primary owner (or the individual nonagency provider), not a criminal record check [S3][S5].
- For an **agency**: its **written criminal records check policy**, copies of its **Secretary of State filings**, and a list of services with policies and procedures [OAC 3701-60-03(B)(3)].
- For an individual **nonagency provider only**: a **notarized affidavit** verifying identity. An LLC agency does not file this affidavit.
- The **$20,000 surety bond** for providers not operating on or just before Sept. 30, 2021 [S1][S5].

Providers certified by the Department of Aging under ORC 173.391 may have certain application items waived [S1].

**Step 4 — File and pay.** The **$250** fee is non-refundable and goes in with the completed application [S3]. OAC 3701-60-03(B)(2) requires a cashier's check or postal money order payable to 'Treasurer, State of Ohio' [S4]. ODH also offers electronic filing and payment through its e-form, which it calls the fastest option [S3]. Mailed applications go to ODH Revenue Processing #3506, P.O. Box 15278, Columbus OH 43215 [S3].

**Step 5 — Respond and wait.** Answer any ODH request for information promptly and confirm the response deadline in writing; the 14-day window and ODH's 60-day status-inquiry guidance were not confirmed against the rule text. The statute says ODH must issue the license once the fee is paid and the statutory requirements are shown, and sets no day count [S1]. A pre-licensure site visit is mandated for applicants relying on the Medicare-certification basis, not for the nonmedical route described in the statute text [S1]. Budget at least 2–3 months from filing to license as a planning assumption, and do not take clients or advertise services before the license is issued.

**After licensure.**

- **Term and renewal.** Renewal costs **$250**. Confirm the license term and the renewal filing deadline with ODH; they were not confirmed against the rule text.
- **Change notice.** Confirm with ODH the deadline for written notice of changes to application information.
- **Penalties.** Operating without a license is a misdemeanor of the second degree on a first offense, per ODH's 2022 rule memo [S7]. ODH may refuse, limit, suspend, revoke or place a license on probation [S1].
- **Rule timing.** Chapter 3701-60 is next scheduled for five-year review on 01/27/2028 [S4]. No pending amendment was found.

**Medicaid add-ons (optional, later).** These steps come after licensure.

- **PASSPORT.** A secondary source says prospective providers must be recommended by a Council on Aging for ODA certification. It also says applicants must already be billing two non-relative clients for at least three months [S8]. The CY2025 application fee reported there was $730; the 2026 figure was not verified [S8]. We could not confirm whether ODA's 2022 suspension of PASSPORT and Assisted Living provider applications has been lifted.
- **Ohio Home Care Waiver / ODM-billed services.** Agency aides must meet the rule 5160-46-04 requirements (see Section 5), including RN/LPN supervision, and the agency must be Medicare-certified or otherwise accredited. These costs are not modeled.
- **Medicaid enrollment.** The 2026 ODM application fee for organizational providers is **$750** (CMS CY2026 federal amount also $750), waived if the fee was paid to Medicare or another state's Medicaid within two years, with proof [S19][S20].
- **Moratorium.** New Medicaid enrollment for home health, hospice and related provider types is paused May 14–Nov. 14, 2026 [S28][S29]. Whether personal care aide and home care attendant types are covered was not confirmed. If they are, no Medicaid billing can start before about Nov. 14, 2026, so plan a private-pay-only bridge. Confirm current status with ODM before applying.
sections.reimbursement:
**How money flows in Ohio.** Ohio has no single 'personal care' payer. Three streams matter.

1. **Private pay.** Families pay the agency directly by the hour. Long-term-care insurance and veterans benefits also pay privately, though this research did not retrieve data on either. Private pay is the only stream fully modeled in the default configuration.
2. **ODA PASSPORT.** PASSPORT is a 1915(c) waiver run by the Department of Aging with ODM, delivered locally through Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) and Councils on Aging. It is not an entitlement and enrollment is slot-limited. An individual needs an open slot that stays within the CMS-authorized limit [S27]. Agencies are certified under OAC 173-39 [S32].
3. **ODM Ohio Home Care Waiver and Medicaid personal care aide.** These are billed through ODM. HCPCS T1019 is the code listed for the personal care aide service [S15]. The home care attendant is billed under S5125 [S13].

**Published rates (latest retrieved sheet, probably superseded).** ODA's rate sheet effective **Jan. 1, 2024** lists [S14]. OAC 5160-1-06.1, which carries the PASSPORT maximum payment rates in its appendix, now shows an effective date of April 17, 2026. The 2026 appendix was not read, so these rates are probably not current.

| Service | Rate (Jan 2024 sheet) |
|---|---|
| PASSPORT personal care, first tier | $7.24 per 15 min ($28.96/hr) |
| PASSPORT personal care, second tier | $5.43 per 15 min |
| PASSPORT consumer-directed personal care | $3.44 per 15 min (second tier $2.58) |
| PASSPORT home care attendant personal care | $4.70 per 15 min (overtime $7.05) |
| PASSPORT homemaker | $5.39 per 15 min |

Under OAC 5160-46-06.1 (effective Jan. 1, 2024), the home care attendant nursing-task service (HCAS/N, S5125) has a $27.53 base rate and a **$6.39** per 15-minute unit rate, with overtime at $9.81 [S13]. That is a medication and nursing-task rate and is outside non-medical scope. Personal care aide tasks are included in the unit rate only when billed under Table A (in lieu of continuous nursing). Under Table B (intermittent nursing), personal-care-only HCAS/PC bills at $4.70 per unit (overtime $7.05, modifier U8) and can be rendered only in conjunction with an HCAS/N service. Do not use $6.39 for personal-care-only revenue. ODM states that PASSPORT and home care waiver fee schedules are set in specific OAC rules and that the current and previous schedules are published there [S16]. The meaning and application of the PASSPORT 'second tier' rate was not verified, so it is not modeled.

**2026 rate uncertainty.** A 2025 Senate testimony described proposed 2% HCBS rate increases as amendments to HB 96 [S24]. A PASSPORT waiver amendment posted Nov. 6, 2025 proposed rate increases effective March 1, 2026 tied to the state budget [S31]. We could not confirm enactment, final amounts, or any 2026 published rate sheet. Rule 5160-46-06 carries an April 17, 2026 effective date, so check medicaid.ohio.gov for the current schedule [S12]. Treat every Medicaid rate in this report as a 2024 reference that is probably superseded, and re-price the PASSPORT lines once the current ODA sheet is in hand.

**Managed care.** MyCare Ohio plans are not bound to pay the same rates as fee-for-service waivers; rates follow each plan's provider contract [S16]. No plan rates are published in the sources reviewed.

**Consumer direction.** A secondary source says the CD-PCS hourly pay rate is set by the state, while C-HCAS lets participants choose rates within a budget [not an ODA/ODM source; treat as unverified]. The ODA sheet's consumer-directed personal care rate ($3.44 per 15 minutes) pays the individual-employer model, not an agency [S14].

**Room and board.** Not applicable to in-home personal care as modeled. The SSI federal benefit rate of $994/month in 2026 is the reference for assisted living maintenance allowances, not in-home care. No in-home room-and-board rule was retrieved.

**Billing mechanics.** ODM says EVV is part of federal law and requires direct care workers to electronically report six items for certain personal care and home health services: service type, recipient, date, location, worker and start/end time [S17]. ODM's state-provided EVV devices and Sandata system are free to providers [S17]. The Ohio Auditor of State reported that Ohio had not yet required EVV as a condition for payment, and ODM said it was phasing in requirements [S18]. Whether EVV is today a condition of payment for all PASSPORT and Home Care Waiver personal care was not confirmed.
sections.demand:
**Demographics.** About **2.27 million** Ohioans were aged 65 and older in 2024, or **19.1%** of the state's population versus 18% nationally (USAFacts, compiled from Census data) [S34]. A population that is older than the national average supports steady demand for in-home help. This is a secondary source, and an official Census 65+ table was not retrieved.

**Medicaid-funded demand.** ODA's waiver data report PASSPORT ending caseload of **18,074 in June 2026**, with a peak in the monthly series of **21,190 in November 2025** [S26]. The same data set shows 13,196 for August 2026, a sharp drop. We could not tell whether that is real or a reporting artifact, so it is not used. PASSPORT enrollment is limited to open slots within the CMS-authorized cap [S27]. Whether a waitlist exists today varies by AAA and must be confirmed locally. A secondary source says PASSPORT has historically had no chronic statewide waitlist; this was not verified against an official source.

**Supply of providers.** Contracted PASSPORT providers numbered **4,115 in August 2026, up from 3,565 in July 2025** [S26]. That is about 15% growth in a year. It means more competition for AAA referrals and for the same slots. The number of ODH-licensed nonmedical agencies was not retrieved.

**Policy demand driver.** ODM states Ohio is one of 47 states plus DC that provides home and community-based care under a CMS waiver, and says home health care costs about half as much as nursing facility placement on average (an agency claim, not independently verified) [S28]. That policy preference supports the waiver system's long-term funding, though it does not guarantee rates or slots.

**Referral sources.** Typical referral sources are:

- Hospital and rehab discharge planners.
- Senior living communities.
- Physicians.
- Elder-law and estate attorneys.
- Families searching online.
- For Medicaid clients, the AAA/Council on Aging care managers, who assign cases from provider lists [S8].

No referral volume data by source were found, and none are claimed.
sections.operations:
**What the licensing rules require.** The ODH sources reviewed do not set nonmedical staffing ratios, awake-overnight rules, administrator qualifications or capacity limits. The verified staffing rules are the threshold of more than two unrelated individuals for nonagency licensure [S1] and, for Older Americans Act personal care under OAC 173-3-06.5, the following [S10]:

- Adequate staffing to provide personal care at least five days per week.
- A back-up plan when no aide is available, which means paid standby capacity.
- A personal care supervisor available during all hours when aides are scheduled to work.
- Initial aide qualifications: STNA, Medicare aide standards, one year of experience plus a competency evaluation, or at least 30 hours of training plus a competency evaluation.
- Licensure under ORC 3740 / OAC 3701-60.

The default model has one supervisor and does not cost after-hours supervisor coverage. Confirm administrator and policy requirements directly with ODH before opening, because the rule text beyond the excerpts reviewed was not retrieved.

**Background checks.** A licensed agency may not employ, or continue to employ, a direct-care worker who fails the database and criminal records screening in ORC 3740.11 [S1]. Screen every direct-care applicant before first client contact. The model carries a per-client cost for checks, which is an operator estimate.

**Aide scope and training.** Requirements differ by payer program.

- **All waiver personal care aides** may not administer prescribed or over-the-counter medications, only help the client self-administer [S11].
- **PASSPORT / Older Americans Act aides (OAC 173-3-06.5):** 6 hours of ODA-approved in-service every 12 months [S10]. The paid wage time (about 6 hours × $16.57 per aide per year) is not separately modeled; the 4% non-billable factor covers travel only. ODA's 2024 comment package says rule 173-39-02.11 then required no ODA pre-service training, while describing a statutory 30-hour pre-service requirement under RC 173.525 [S9]. The enacted text was not retrieved. Ask your AAA and ODA what applies before hiring PASSPORT aides.
- **ODM Ohio Home Care Waiver agency aides (OAC 5160-46-04):** 8 hours of in-service within 12 months, first-aid certification, and a certificate from an ODH-approved or Medicare aide competency program. Agency aides must be supervised by a licensed RN or LPN, with a face-to-face home visit at least every 60 days, and the agency must be Medicare-certified or otherwise accredited. The 6-hour in-service in that rule applies only to non-agency aides. None of these Home Care Waiver costs is modeled, and the $46,000 unlicensed supervisor would have to be replaced with RN/LPN supervision at RN/LPN wages if the agency bills ODM.
- Home health aide certification rules outside these programs were not verified. A non-medical aide generally does not need that credential, but confirm if you plan any home-health-type services.

**Wages and labor law.** The Ohio minimum wage is **$11.00** in 2026 for non-tipped employees. It applies to employers above $405,000 in annual gross receipts; smaller employers stay at the federal floor [S25]. Employers must post the 2026 minimum wage poster [S25]. The modeled aide wage ($16.57) is above both. The model does not include an overtime premium or aide mileage between clients; the ODA rate sheet has separate overtime rates, so budget an overtime allowance and mileage reimbursement as operator estimates. A secondary source reports no Ohio city or county sets a higher local minimum; verify locally.

**EVV and systems.** Medicaid personal care visits must be recorded in EVV [S15][S17]. ODM provides Sandata and state devices at no cost [S17]. An alternate EVV vendor would be at the provider's own cost, and ODM paused alternate-vendor applications on May 13, 2026 [S17]. ODM has also said it will file rules requiring GPS for all EVV providers and begin rulemaking on live-in caregiver EVV; adoption was not verified [S28]. Private-pay scheduling, billing and payroll software is not covered by the state and is a modeled cost.

**Office team.** The default agency uses a full-time administrator, one client care supervisor (intake assessments, care plans, aide orientation, supervisory visits) and one scheduler/billing coordinator. These roles and ratios are operator estimates, not ODH rule requirements for a private-pay agency.

**Payroll burden.** The model uses 9.5% payroll taxes, 3% workers' compensation and 3% benefits. All three are operator estimates. Ohio workers' compensation is a state monopoly fund through BWC, and no class rate for personal care aides was retrieved. Official ODJFS unemployment rates were not verified because secondary sources conflicted. At about 55 FTEs, the 100-client PASSPORT configuration would exceed the 50-FTE ACA employer threshold (operator calculation), and no employer health-coverage cost is modeled.
sections.market_conditions:
**Private-pay prices.** Genworth/CareScout's 2024 national medians are **$34/hour** for home health aide services and **$33/hour** for homemaker services, with the homemaker figure up 10% from 2023 [S21]. The survey measures standard hourly private rates and is not specific to a metro area. For Ohio, a secondary guide citing CareScout reports about **$33/hour homemaker and $32/hour home health aide** in 2024 [S22]. Another secondary page citing Genworth reports a **$28** Ohio average for non-medical home care, with urban areas at $32–$36 [S23]. Official Ohio-specific 2025 CareScout figures were not retrieved. The model uses $33 as the default and $28 as the low case. Price against local competitor quotes before committing.

**Wages.** The national BLS median for home health and personal care aides was **$35,800 a year ($17.21/hour)** in May 2025 [S35]. A third-party table citing BLS OEWS puts the Ohio median at **$34,460 ($16.57/hour)** [S36]. Official Ohio OEWS tables were not fetched. Because Ohio's statewide median is a blend of rural and metro markets, an agency in Columbus, Cleveland or Cincinnati may have to pay above $16.57 to hire and keep aides. Each extra $1.00 an hour in aide pay costs about $3,000 a month in the default configuration (Section 8).

**Medicaid rate context.** The PASSPORT first-tier rate of $28.96/hour (2024 sheet) is about $4 below the modeled private price [S14][S22]. A Medicaid hour is therefore worth less to the agency than a private-pay hour while costing the same aide wage. Whether 2026 increases took effect is unverified [S24][S31].

**Supply and competition.** Contracted PASSPORT providers rose from 3,565 to 4,115 between July 2025 and August 2026 [S26]. The count of licensed nonmedical agencies and market shares were not found and are not claimed.

**Regulatory and enforcement climate in 2026.** ODM paused new Medicaid enrollment for home health and related types from May 14 to Nov. 14, 2026 [S28][S29]. It suspended payments to 49 high-risk Medicaid home health providers in June 2026 [S30]. An executive order authorized emergency rules for more frequent revalidation of higher-risk providers [S28]. Senate Bill 315 requires EVV program updates [S17]. Private-pay agencies are least exposed to these changes; Medicaid-dependent agencies are most exposed.
sections.financial_narrative:
**How the P&L is built.** Each configuration multiplies clients by occupancy, then revenue per client by payer mix and rate. Caregiver pay scales with census (hours per client-month × wage × 1.155 burden). Office staff, rent, insurance, software, marketing and licensing are fixed. Per-client costs cover software, liability exposure, background checks, recruiting, supplies, mileage and payment processing. The default occupancy is 90% (80% conservative, 95% optimistic). That is an operator assumption, not a sourced statistic. No Ohio utilization data for personal care agencies exist in our sources. Break-even occupancy and first-profit month are computed by the generator from the configuration.

**Results at default occupancy.**

| Configuration | Net / month | Margin | Break-even occupancy | First profit month | Cash needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Private pay, 35 clients (default) | $9,942 | 12.0% | 59.6% | 9 | $89,381 |
| Private pay, 20 clients (owner-administrator) | $5,560 | 11.7% | 60.2% | 7 | $42,519 |
| Mixed, 60 clients (50% private / 50% PASSPORT) | $7,962 | 6.7% | 71.1% | 13 | $200,878 |
| PASSPORT only, 100 clients | $2,840 | 1.8% | 83.9% | 19 | $398,450 |
| Private pay, 35 clients at $28/hour | -$2,469 | -3.5% | 103.1% | never | $202,705 |

**Why the default works, and how thin it is.** At $33/hour the agency earns revenue of about $83,160 a month at 31.5 active clients and 80 hours each (operator estimate — verify locally). A paid aide hour costs roughly $19.90 once the 4% non-billable time and 15.5% burden are applied to $16.57/hour. That leaves about $13 per billable hour, or roughly $930 per client-month after per-client costs. About $19,450 a month of fixed office cost (salaries with burden plus rent, insurance, software, marketing and licensing) absorbs about 21 active clients before profit begins. Everything above that is the 12% margin. The salaried team is paid in full in every month, including the owner-administrator at the 20-client size.

**Sensitivities (hand-calculated from the model's inputs; approximate).**

- **Price.** Each $1.00 per hour changes net by about **$2,500 a month** at 31.5 clients. At $28 the 35-client agency loses about $2,469 a month. Break-even price at 90% census is therefore roughly **$29/hour**. We did not lower wages or staffing to make the $28 case profitable.
- **Aide wage.** Each $1.00 per hour changes net by about **$3,000 a month**. At $17.57 the default nets roughly $6,900. The Ohio median is statewide, so metro agencies should test a higher wage.
- **Hours per client.** The 80 hours per client-month is an operator estimate — verify locally. If clients average 60 hours instead, net falls to roughly **$2,000 a month** and break-even rises to about 29 active clients (about 82% of capacity), because fixed office cost does not shrink.
- **Occupancy.** At 80% the default nets roughly $6,700 a month; at 95% roughly $11,600.

**Medicaid economics.** PASSPORT personal care at $7.24 per 15 minutes pays $28.96/hour (2024 sheet) [S14]. That is about $4 below the private price against an identical aide wage, so each Medicaid hour contributes roughly $9 instead of $13. The mixed agency reaches only 6.7% margin and 71.1% break-even occupancy. The PASSPORT-only agency reaches 1.8% and needs 83.9% occupancy, so a modest drop in census or a pay-rate change erases the profit. The model uses 60 billable hours per PASSPORT client-month, which is also an operator estimate because PASSPORT hours are not published in the sources reviewed. The $5.43 second-tier rate and T1019 are not modeled, and 2026 rate increases are not assumed [S14][S24][S31]. If the second tier applies to part of the units, real revenue would be lower than modeled.

**Cash.** The modeled cash need includes startup costs and the ramp-up deficit while census builds. It runs from $42,519 for the 20-client owner-run agency to $89,381 for the default, $200,878 for the mixed agency and $398,450 for PASSPORT-only. Medicaid agencies should hold more because of slow payment risk, the 2026 payment suspensions [S30] and billing-history prerequisites [S8].

**Path to profit.** Launch private pay at 20–35 clients and price at or above $33/hour only if local competitor quotes support it. Control aide hours and wage drift. Reach about 21 active clients at 80 hours (about 29 at 60 hours) to cover the office team. Add Medicaid only after the license, a private-pay client base and a stable cash cushion are in place.
sections.risks:
**Pricing risk.** The $33/hour price comes from a secondary source citing 2024 survey data [S22]. Another secondary page puts the Ohio average at $28 [S23]. Neither was checked against the primary CareScout data. At $28 the default agency loses money at every occupancy up to 100% [model result]. Pricing is the single biggest risk.

**Wage risk.** The Ohio median aide wage ($16.57) is a statewide figure from a third-party table and was not confirmed on a BLS state page [S36]. The median is a midpoint, not an entry wage. Urban agencies may pay more. Each $1.00 per hour costs about $3,000 a month at the default size. The state minimum wage is $11.00 [S25], so wages are not constrained by it, but the labor market is.

**Utilization risk.** The 80 hours per client-month and 90% occupancy are operator estimates. If clients average 60 hours, the default nets roughly $2,000 a month (Section 8). Hospitalizations, deaths and client turnover drive occupancy, and recruiting is continuous.

**Licensing and compliance risk.**

- Operating without a license is a misdemeanor of the second degree on a first offense [S7].
- ODH may refuse, limit, suspend, revoke or place a license on probation [S1].
- Missed deadlines hurt. Confirm with ODH the response window for application requests, the deadline for reporting changes and the renewal filing deadline; those details were not confirmed against the rule text.
- Aides who fail ORC 3740.11 screening cannot be employed in direct-care roles [S1].
- Medicaid-billed work carries added staffing rules that the model does not cost: RN/LPN supervision, 8-hour in-service, first-aid and competency requirements and Medicare certification or accreditation for ODM Home Care Waiver agencies (OAC 5160-46-04); and a supervisor available during all scheduled hours, a back-up aide plan, pre-service training or competency evaluation and 6 hours of paid in-service for PASSPORT aides (OAC 173-3-06.5).
- Rules that were not retrieved, such as ODH administrator qualifications, could create costs the model does not include.

**Medicaid access and policy risk.**

- New Medicaid enrollment for home health, hospice and related provider types is paused through Nov. 14, 2026 [S28][S29]. Whether personal care aide and home care attendant types are covered was not confirmed. If they are, no Medicaid billing can start before about that date. Whether the pause will be extended is unknown.
- The PASSPORT rates used ($7.24 per 15 minutes) come from a Jan 2024 sheet that is probably superseded; OAC 5160-1-06.1 now shows an April 17, 2026 effective date [S14]. The PASSPORT-only and mixed margins (1.8% and 6.7%) could move either way.
- PASSPORT certification may require Council on Aging recommendation and two non-relative paying clients for three months [S8]. ODA's 2022 suspension of provider applications was not confirmed lifted.
- PASSPORT enrollment is slot-limited [S27]. Provider count grew about 15% in a year [S26].
- The August 2026 caseload figure (13,196, versus 18,074 in June) is unexplained [S26].
- Managed care plans can pay below fee-for-service rates [S16].

**Program-integrity risk.** ODM suspended payments to 49 high-risk home health providers in June 2026 [S30] and plans emergency revalidation rules [S28]. EVV rules are tightening, including planned GPS requirements and live-in caregiver EVV; alternate-vendor processing is paused [S17][S28]. Missing EVV data could mean denied or delayed payment. A GPS-based EVV change could also require new devices or software.

**Cost-estimate risk.** Many costs (office rent, insurance, software, supervisor and administrator salaries, payroll burden, surety premium) are operator estimates. The model also omits overtime premium, aide mileage, standby back-up aides and, at 100 clients, possible ACA employer coverage. Get quotes before relying on the default result.
sections.recommendations:
1. **Confirm the facts with ODH before filing.** Call or email ODH Home Health Agency Licensure to confirm administrator and policy requirements, insurance expectations, the license term, renewal deadline and the current processing time. We could not find an ODH phone number or email in our sources [S5]. Confirm which exemptions might apply [S33].

2. **Start private pay, 20 to 35 clients.** The default 35-client private-pay agency is the only modeled agency with an adequate margin and a manageable cash need ($89,381, first profit month 9). If capital is tight, start with the 20-client owner-administrator model ($42,519 cash, first profit month 7), recognizing that the owner is also the supervisor and works a full week.

3. **Test price in the market before you sign a lease.** Collect rate sheets or quotes from at least five local agencies. Use $33/hour only if local competitors support it [S22]. If the local market is closer to $28 [S23], do not open with this staffing model. At that price the 35-client agency does not break even at any occupancy up to 100%. Roughly $29/hour is the break-even price in the model.

4. **Control the two large cost drivers.** Aide wage and billable hours per client decide the result. Track hours per client monthly and refuse low-hour cases that do not cover scheduling and supervision costs. Pay at or above the Ohio median of $16.57 only if the price supports it, and expect entry hires to start lower and metro markets higher.

5. **Build cash for the full ramp-up.** Hold the modeled cash need, not just the advisory working capital line in startup costs. Admit clients steadily. Marketing to hospital discharge planners, senior living communities and elder-law attorneys is the main private-pay referral channel; no referral volume data support a specific plan.

6. **Add Medicaid later and deliberately.** Wait for the ODM moratorium to end or be clarified (Nov. 14, 2026), and ask ODM whether personal care aide and home care attendant provider types are covered [S28][S29]. Ask your Council on Aging whether PASSPORT provider applications are open, what the current 2026 application fee is, and how many non-relative billing months are required [S8]. Pull the current PASSPORT rate appendix (OAC 5160-1-06.1, effective April 17, 2026) and any MCO contract rates in writing, and re-price before modeling. Cost the added requirements: RN/LPN supervision and Medicare certification or accreditation for Home Care Waiver billing, after-hours supervisor coverage and back-up aides for PASSPORT, and paid training and in-service time. At the 2024 rates the mixed agency earns 6.7% and the PASSPORT-only agency 1.8% before those added costs, so Medicaid is worth adding only if rates have risen or you have spare supervised capacity.

7. **Build compliance in from day one.** Confirm and calendar the ODH renewal, response and change-notice deadlines. Run ORC 3740.11 screening on every aide [S1]. Train Medicaid aides on the in-service hours that apply to their program (6 hours for PASSPORT under OAC 173-3-06.5; 8 hours plus first aid for Home Care Waiver agency aides under OAC 5160-46-04) and on the no-medication-administration rule [S10][S11]. Use Ohio's free Sandata EVV and devices for any Medicaid visits [S17]. Watch ODM announcements for GPS EVV, revalidation and prior-authorization changes [S28].

8. **Do not remove required costs to make the numbers work.** The $20,000 surety bond, $250 license fees, background checks, EVV and in-service training are real costs [S1][S5][S10]. The model keeps them.

The 100-client PASSPORT configuration would have about 55 FTEs at full census, above the 50-FTE threshold (operator calculation, not a retrieved source). None of these is modeled, and the 3% benefits estimate is unverified.

The $4.70 unit rate (overtime $7.05, modifier U8) can be billed only in conjunction with an HCAS/N service, and the $6.39 HCAS/N rate is a nursing-task rate outside non-medical scope; neither is modeled as personal care revenue.

checklist.task: Confirm that Ohio requires a nonmedical home health license for your business model
checklist.instructions: Ohio does have a general nonmedical home care license. Beginning October 1, 2022, no home health agency or nonagency provider may provide nonmedical home health services without a license. Do not rely on blogs or older hints saying Ohio has no such license. Read ORC Chapter 3740 and OAC Chapter 3701-60 before spending money. Cost: free. Time: 2–3 hours.

checklist.task: Decide whether you are an agency or a 'nonagency provider' and confirm the two-person threshold
checklist.instructions: A self-employed individual who provides direct care to not more than two individuals who are not immediate family members is excluded from the nonagency definition. Above that count, a license is required. An agency that employs caregivers needs the license regardless. Write down your intended structure (employer agency vs. solo provider) before you apply.

checklist.task: Check whether you fall under a licensure exemption
checklist.instructions: ODH lists some entities that do not need the nonmedical license, for example providers certified by the Department of Developmental Disabilities under ORC Chapter 5123. Review the ODH Home Health Agencies page and confirm in writing (email ODH) if you think an exemption applies. Do not assume an exemption covers private-pay personal care. Cost: free.
checklist.cite: ORC 3740.01; ODH Home Health Agencies page

checklist.task: Understand the penalty for operating without a license
checklist.instructions: ODH's 2022 rule memo states that operating without a required license is a misdemeanor of the second degree on a first offense. Do not accept clients, advertise services or place caregivers until the license is issued. Keep the license copy on file.
checklist.cite: ORC Chapter 3740; ODH rule memo (3701-60-01 to -11)

checklist.task: Choose your revenue strategy: private pay first, Medicaid later
checklist.instructions: The model's default is a 35-client private-pay agency: about $9,942/month net (12% margin) at 90% census, break-even near 59.6% occupancy, first profit in month 9, and about $89,381 cash needed. The 20-client owner-run model nets about $5,560/month (11.7% margin) with about $42,519 cash needed. Medicaid-heavy models are thinner. The 100-client PASSPORT-only model nets about $2,840/month (1.8% margin) and needs about $398,450. These results rest on operator estimates and unverified 2026 rates, so check them against your own market.

checklist.task: Form an Ohio legal entity (LLC recommended)
checklist.instructions: File Articles of Organization with the Ohio Secretary of State (online filing). A $99 filing fee is reported by secondary sources only, so confirm the current fee on the Secretary of State's site. Optional name reservation is reported at $39 for 180 days (secondary). Time: same day to a few business days. The entity name must match what you put on the ODH application, bond and insurance.
checklist.cite: ORC Chapter 1706 (LLC filing); verify on Ohio Secretary of State site

checklist.task: Obtain a federal EIN
checklist.instructions: Apply free at irs.gov; the number is issued immediately online. You need it for payroll, banking, the surety bond, insurance and Medicaid enrollment.

checklist.task: Draft an operating agreement and open a business bank account
checklist.instructions: Document ownership percentages. ODH asks about owners, and the primary owner must supply fingerprints. Open a dedicated account for payroll and operating funds. Cost: attorney drafting is an operator estimate of $500–$2,000 — verify locally.

checklist.task: Check local zoning and business registration for your office
checklist.instructions: Zoning and siting requirements for home care offices were not researched to a primary source. Call the city or county zoning office for your planned address and ask whether a home-based or commercial office is allowed. A home-based office can be a lean option for a 20-client start. Get the answer in writing.

checklist.task: Download and read the ODH Nonmedical Home Health Services License Application
checklist.instructions: Use the ODH application page for the current form and instructions. ODH accepts the completed application plus a non-refundable fee submitted together. ODH describes electronic filing (Option 1) as the fastest. Read all instructions before you start filling in anything.

checklist.task: Confirm you meet (or are exempt from) the $20,000 surety bond requirement
checklist.instructions: Providers that were not operating on or just before September 30, 2021 must post a $20,000 surety bond issued by a company licensed to do business in Ohio. ODH's licensure page lists the Nonmedical Home Health Services Surety Bond at $20,000. A new business is almost certainly in the bond group.

checklist.task: Obtain the $20,000 surety bond on the ODH form
checklist.instructions: Get quotes from at least two Ohio-licensed surety agents. Use the ODH surety bond form from the ODH licensure page. The premium is an operator estimate of about $200–$800 up front and about $400/year (model uses $33.33/month) — get an actual quote. The bond must be in the legal name of the licensee. Time: usually a few days.

checklist.task: Prepare the notarized affidavit verifying the applicant's identity
checklist.instructions: The application must include a notarized affidavit verifying the applicant's identity. Get it notarized at a bank, library or notary service. Cost: usually under $25 per notarization (operator estimate; fees vary).

checklist.task: Complete fingerprinting for the primary owner
checklist.instructions: ODH requires a fingerprint impression card from the primary owner (or the individual nonagency provider). It does not accept a criminal records check in its place. Use the ODH-specified fingerprint card or process from the application page. Cost: an operator estimate of $25–$75 — verify locally.

checklist.task: Write the days-and-hours-of-operation statement
checklist.instructions: The application must include a statement identifying the days and hours of operation for the applicant. Decide your office and service hours first. If you also plan Older Americans Act personal care, note that staffing must cover personal care at least five days a week.

checklist.task: Gather the remaining application items listed in ORC 3740.03(B)
checklist.instructions: Read ORC 3740.03(B)(1) line by line and build a checklist of every required item. Some of these items may be waived for providers already certified by the Department of Aging under ORC 173.391 (see the PASSPORT note later in this checklist). Ask ODH if any item is unclear. Missing items delay the application.

checklist.task: Ask ODH about administrator qualifications and staffing rules
checklist.instructions: The research found no administrator qualifications, training hours, staffing ratios or capacity limits for nonmedical licensees in the OAC 3701-60 text reviewed. Read the full chapter, then confirm with ODH Home Health Agency Licensure in writing. ODH's phone number and email were not found on the pages reviewed, so use the contact route on the ODH licensure page.

checklist.task: Understand that the pre-license site visit applies to the Medicare-certification route
checklist.instructions: The statute requires a site visit for applicants seeking a license on the Medicare-certification basis. The nonmedical route described in the text does not mention one. Still keep your office, files and policies ready in case ODH asks to inspect after licensure.

checklist.task: Create a license-application working folder with deadlines
checklist.instructions: Track: application date, check or e-payment confirmation, copy of bond, notarized affidavit, fingerprint card receipt and your 14-day response deadline for ODH requests. Keep copies of everything you submit.

checklist.task: Pay the $250 non-refundable application fee with the application
checklist.instructions: Submit the $250 fee together with the completed application. By mail, pay with a cashier's check or postal money order payable to 'Treasurer, State of Ohio'. Electronically, pay by credit card or electronic check through the ODH e-form. The fee is non-refundable even if the application is denied.

checklist.task: File the application (electronic preferred; mail is the alternative)
checklist.instructions: Electronic: use the ODH e-form option, which ODH calls the fastest. By mail: send to ODH Revenue Processing #3506, P.O. Box 15278, Columbus, OH 43215, with the cashier's check or money order. Keep tracking proof if you mail it. Cost: $250 plus postage.

checklist.task: Answer any ODH request for information within 14 days
checklist.instructions: The applicant is obliged to furnish any requested information within fourteen days after the mailing date of the request. Check your email and mail daily after filing. Reply fast, with proof of delivery, and ask for the mailing date of the request.

checklist.task: Plan for roughly 60 days of processing before asking about status
checklist.instructions: ODH's Q&A asks applicants to allow 60 days for processing before contacting ODH about status. The statute sets no day limit; ODH must issue the license once the fee is paid and the statutory requirements are shown. A secondary blog cites 90 days, which conflicts, so budget 60–90 days. Do not start serving clients until you hold the license.

checklist.task: Note the 3-year license term and set a renewal reminder
checklist.instructions: The license lasts three years. Renewal costs $250. A renewal is timely only if filed at least 90 days before the license expires. Put the deadline in your calendar the day the license is issued, with a second reminder 120 days before expiration.

checklist.task: Set up a 10-day written change-notice procedure
checklist.instructions: Licensees must give written notice to ODH within ten days of changes to application information (for example owner, address, name, contact). Assign one person to send notices and keep copies.

checklist.task: Post and file the license; use it correctly in marketing
checklist.instructions: Keep the license on file at the office. Use the exact licensed legal name in contracts, advertising and invoices. Confirm with ODH whether any posting requirement exists in OAC 3701-60.

checklist.task: Know ODH's enforcement powers
checklist.instructions: ODH may refuse to issue, limit, suspend or revoke a license, or place it on probation. Build a compliance routine from day one (screening, records, timely notices) so the license is never at risk.

checklist.task: Calendar the scheduled five-year review of Chapter 3701-60
checklist.instructions: The next scheduled five-year review of OAC Chapter 3701-60 is 01/27/2028, with no pending change found in sources reviewed. Check the Ohio Administrative Code site every six months for amendments.

checklist.task: Register with Ohio BWC for workers' compensation coverage
checklist.instructions: Ohio operates a monopoly state fund through the Bureau of Workers' Compensation, so private carriers do not write standard coverage. Apply through BWC before your first employee starts. The model uses a 3% payroll estimate because no BWC class rate for personal care aides was retrieved. Get your actual class code and rate from BWC. The generic average of $0.74 per $100 payroll is not a home care class rate. BWC announced an average 1% private-employer rate cut effective July 1, 2026 (secondary reports).

checklist.task: Register as an Ohio employer for unemployment insurance (ODJFS)
checklist.instructions: Register before first payroll. The official 2026 new-employer rate and taxable wage base were not verified; secondary sources conflict (2.7% vs 2.85%; $9,000 vs $9,500). Get your assigned rate from ODJFS. The model's 9.5% payroll-tax assumption is an operator estimate — verify locally.

checklist.task: Set up payroll withholding and employer tax accounts
checklist.instructions: Register for federal withholding and FICA through your payroll system. Set up Ohio state and municipal income tax withholding as employee deductions. Municipal tax rates vary by city (secondary sources show Columbus at 2.50%). Use a payroll service; the model budgets accounting/payroll/legal at $700/month (operator estimate).

checklist.task: Buy general and professional liability, hired/non-owned auto and crime coverage
checklist.instructions: The research found no ODH insurance minimum beyond the $20,000 surety bond. Referral partners, families and payers may still require limits. Get at least two quotes from a broker experienced in home care. The model uses $500/month base plus $15 per client (operator estimates). Ask about abuse/molestation, employee dishonesty (crime) and non-owned auto cover.

checklist.task: Fund the cash reserve for ramp-up before you open
checklist.instructions: Model cash needs: about $42,519 (20-client private pay), $89,381 (35-client private pay), $200,878 (60-client mixed) and $398,450 (100-client PASSPORT-only). The 35-client private-pay model does not turn a profit until month 9. These figures use operator-estimate ramp assumptions (2–3 new clients per month). Arrange a line of credit or owner capital before applying.

checklist.task: Stress-test your pricing before signing a lease
checklist.instructions: The model prices private pay at $33/hour (CareYaya, citing Genworth/CareScout 2024, a secondary source). The national CareScout median is $33 homemaker and $34 home health aide. A third-party page reports a $28 Ohio average, $32–$36 in urban areas. At $28/hour the 35-client model loses about $2,469/month and cannot break even even at 100% occupancy. Call 5–10 local competitors for their real hourly rates and adjust.

checklist.task: Choose scheduling, billing and EVV-interface software
checklist.instructions: Get demos and quotes (the model assumes $300/month base plus $12 per client, operator estimates). If you will bill Medicaid later, confirm the software can interface with Ohio's Sandata EVV system. Ohio's state EVV system and devices are free to Medicaid providers. Private-pay scheduling and billing software is your cost.

checklist.task: Build the office: lease, phones, IT and furnishings
checklist.instructions: The model's default office is about 1,000 sq ft at $1,500/month (operator estimate). HUD residential Fair Market Rents are not an office-rent benchmark. Rent is a fixed cost even when census is low. Negotiate a short initial term or a flexible lease while census is small.

checklist.task: Use a lawyer or consultant to review your license application and contracts
checklist.instructions: The model budgets $1,000–$4,000 (operator estimate) for attorney or consultant review of license and enrollment paperwork. Also have the client service agreement and employment documents reviewed for Ohio law.

checklist.task: Pay at least the Ohio minimum wage and plan wages above it
checklist.instructions: Ohio's 2026 minimum wage is $11.00/hour for non-tipped employees. The state rate applies to businesses above $405,000 in annual gross receipts; smaller employers stay on the federal floor. No Ohio city or county sets a higher local minimum wage (secondary source). The model uses $16.57/hour (Ohio median home health and personal care aide pay per a CareSlink table citing BLS OEWS May 2025). The national BLS median is $17.21/hour. Check local job postings before you set your pay scale.

checklist.task: Display the official 2026 Ohio minimum wage poster
checklist.instructions: The Department of Commerce states employers are required to display the official 2026 Minimum Wage poster. Download it from the Commerce site and post it where employees can see it. For field staff, confirm with your lawyer how to provide it (for example, in the office and in the onboarding packet).
checklist.cite: Ohio Dept. of Commerce 2026 minimum wage notice

checklist.task: Screen every direct-care applicant under ORC 3740.11 before hire
checklist.instructions: A home health agency may not employ an applicant, or continue to employ an employee, in a position involving direct care if the database and criminal records screening under ORC 3740.11 disqualifies them. The research verified only the opening prohibition, not the full database list or BCI/FBI specifics. Read ORC 3740.11 in full and build a screening procedure. Cost: the model budgets $8 per client per month for checks (operator estimate).

checklist.task: Document the screening result for each employee and recheck as required
checklist.instructions: Keep each employee's screening result in a personnel file. Re-screen on the schedule set in ORC 3740.11 and OAC 3701-60. Remove from direct care immediately anyone who becomes disqualified.

checklist.task: Write job descriptions that match what nonmedical caregivers may do
checklist.instructions: ORC 3740.01 defines nonmedical services to include personal care and assistance managing the individual's home and handling personal affairs. Limit duties to the licensed scope. Under Ohio Home Care Waiver rules, personal care aides do not administer prescribed or over-the-counter medications; they may only help the client self-administer. Use the same rule in private-pay policies unless your lawyer advises otherwise.

checklist.task: Confirm training requirements for aides you will use
checklist.instructions: Ohio home health aide certification and training rules were not verified. Medicaid personal care aides must complete six hours of in-service education annually. ODA's 2024 comment package said OAC 173-39-02.11 then required no pre-service training, while RC 173.525 proposed a 30-hour pre-service requirement for PASSPORT aides; the enacted text was not retrieved. Check the current text of OAC 173-39-02.11 and call the Area Agency on Aging before hiring for PASSPORT.

checklist.task: Hire and train an administrator/supervisor structure
checklist.instructions: No ODH administrator qualification was found in the rules reviewed. Confirm with ODH. The model uses a $60,000 administrator, a $46,000 client care supervisor and a $38,000 scheduler/billing coordinator for 35 clients (all operator estimates — verify locally). A 20-client start uses an owner-administrator at $55,000 plus a half-time scheduler.

checklist.task: Plan caregiver hours, travel time and overtime
checklist.instructions: The model assumes 80 billable hours per client per month plus 4% paid non-billable time (operator estimates — verify locally). Pay for travel between clients as required by wage-hour law, and keep daily time records. Check your overtime exposure with a payroll provider.

checklist.task: Build a recruiting pipeline and a turnover budget
checklist.instructions: The model budgets $25 per client per month for recruiting and onboarding (operator estimate). Caregiver turnover is a main cost driver. Offer reliable hours, mileage handling and a clear schedule to keep staff.

checklist.task: Write your policies and procedures manual
checklist.instructions: Cover intake, service scope, abuse/neglect reporting, incident reports, complaint handling, emergency procedures, infection control and records retention. Read OAC Chapter 3701-60 for any mandatory policy content before drafting. The model budgets $1,500–$6,000 for the manual and forms (operator estimate). Time: 2–4 weeks.

checklist.task: Create the client service agreement and consent packet
checklist.instructions: Include hourly rate, minimum visit length, cancellation terms, billing cycle, client rights, scope of services and the no-medication-administration rule. Have an Ohio attorney review it.

checklist.task: Develop the intake assessment and written care plan process
checklist.instructions: Each new client gets an in-home assessment by the supervisor, a written plan of care and a caregiver match. Record any safety concerns. Review plans regularly (operator practice — verify any rule-based frequency in OAC 3701-60).

checklist.task: Set up caregiver orientation and ongoing in-service training
checklist.instructions: Create an orientation covering personal care tasks, safe transfers, dementia communication, infection control, emergency response and documentation. Track at least six hours of annual in-service per aide, which is mandatory for Medicaid personal care aides and a sensible standard for private pay. The model budgets $150/month for training materials (operator estimate).

checklist.task: Create an on-call and schedule-coverage system
checklist.instructions: Set up a way to cover call-offs. If you will also deliver personal care under Older Americans Act contracts, your staffing must be adequate to provide personal care at least five days per week. Decide your on-call rotation and your backup caregivers.

checklist.task: Set up client and employee record systems with confidentiality controls
checklist.instructions: Store client records, time records, screening results and training logs securely. Use access controls and backups. Written retention periods should match OAC 3701-60 and your lawyer's advice.

checklist.task: Buy PPE, supplies and caregiver kits
checklist.instructions: The model budgets $8 per client per month for gloves, PPE and care supplies (operator estimate). Include a first-aid kit and disinfectants in each caregiver's kit.

checklist.task: Set your hourly price from local competitor research
checklist.instructions: Benchmarks: $33/hour Ohio homemaker and $32/hour home health aide (CareYaya citing Genworth/CareScout 2024, secondary); $28/hour Ohio average non-medical with $32–$36 in urban areas (Paying for Senior Care, secondary); national CareScout median $33 homemaker and $34 aide. These are 2024 figures and may not match your metro. Call competitors posing as a client to get real prices. Do not drop below the price that covers wages and fixed costs.

checklist.task: Estimate local demand before choosing your service area
checklist.instructions: USAFacts reports about 2.27 million Ohioans aged 65+ in 2024 (19.1% of the population vs. 18% nationally). The senior population grew more than 10% from 2020 to 2024 per Census Vintage 2024 reports. Use county-level Census data to pick a service area where seniors are concentrated and competitors are fewer. No provider counts or market shares were verified.

checklist.task: Build referral relationships
checklist.instructions: Target hospital and rehab discharge planners, senior living communities, elder-law and estate attorneys, care managers, physician offices and faith groups. Budget $1,500–$2,000/month for marketing (operator estimate). Referral volumes were not verified; track your own conversion rates.

checklist.task: Launch a website and Google Business Profile with accurate licensing language
checklist.instructions: State that you are licensed by the Ohio Department of Health as a nonmedical home health services provider only after the license is issued. Do not advertise medical or skilled services. Cost: the model budgets $2,000–$8,000 for launch marketing and a website (operator estimate).

checklist.task: Check long-term care insurance, VA and Area Agency on Aging private-pay channels
checklist.instructions: Ask long-term care insurers about their vendor requirements and billing formats. Contact your local Area Agency on Aging about Older Americans Act personal care contracts, which carry a five-day-per-week staffing adequacy rule. Terms vary; none were verified here.

checklist.task: Set up client invoicing and payment collection
checklist.instructions: Offer ACH and card payments. The model assumes about 1.5% blended payment-processing cost (operator estimate). Bill weekly or biweekly; collect a deposit if your lawyer approves.

checklist.task: Track monthly KPIs against the model
checklist.instructions: Track active clients, billable hours, gross margin per hour, caregiver turnover, overtime, referral source and days to collect. The 35-client model breaks even near 59.6% occupancy; at 90% occupancy it nets about $9,942/month. If you are below break-even by month 6, re-check price and hours.

checklist.task: Check the Ohio Medicaid new-enrollment moratorium before planning any Medicaid billing
checklist.instructions: ODM has paused new Medicaid enrollment for home health, hospice and related provider types, including personal care aides and home care attendants, effective May 14 through November 14, 2026. Check the ODM program integrity page for extensions or changes before you apply. Plan a private-pay launch that does not depend on Medicaid.

checklist.task: Understand PASSPORT provider certification steps
checklist.instructions: Per the Council on Aging of Southwestern Ohio (secondary), businesses must be recommended by a Council on Aging for certification by ODA, and must already be billing and receiving payment from two non-relative clients for at least three months. A 2022 notice said ODA suspended the PASSPORT and Assisted Living provider application process; whether it has been lifted is unverified. Call your Area Agency on Aging for current status. Read OAC 173-39-02.11 for personal care certification requirements.

checklist.task: Ask ODH about the paperwork waiver for ODA-certified providers
checklist.instructions: The director of health shall waive receipt of certain application items under ORC 3740.03(B)(1)(a)–(g) for providers certified by the Department of Aging under ORC 173.391. Ask ODH how this applies if you are certified before you apply for the nonmedical license.

checklist.task: Budget the PASSPORT certification fee and the Medicaid application fee
checklist.instructions: The PASSPORT application fee was $730 for CY2025 (secondary); the 2026 fee is not verified, so ask the Council on Aging. Ohio Medicaid charges organizational providers $750 per application for 2026, and the fee is waived if you paid Medicare or another state's Medicaid within two years (proof required). The Medicaid fee is paid at application.

checklist.task: Prepare the Ohio Medicaid provider enrollment application (when the moratorium allows)
checklist.instructions: A third-party guide says enrollment runs through the PNM module with an OH|ID login and no paper applications. Rules under OAC Chapter 5160-45 (provider agreement) were not retrieved, so read them before applying. Expect more frequent revalidation of higher-risk providers under Executive Order 2026-01D.

checklist.task: Verify current Medicaid rates before modeling any Medicaid revenue
checklist.instructions: The latest rate sheet retrieved is effective January 1, 2024: PASSPORT personal care $7.24 per 15 minutes (second tier $5.43); Ohio Home Care Waiver HCAS/N S5125 $6.39 per unit. A 2% HCBS increase was proposed in HB 96, and a PASSPORT amendment proposed rate increases effective March 1, 2026; neither is confirmed. No published T1019 rate was found. Managed care plans (MyCare) are not bound to fee-for-service rates. Check the ODM Schedules and Rates page and ODA rate sheets for current figures.

checklist.task: Test the Medicaid financial case before committing
checklist.instructions: At the 2024 rate, the 60-client mixed model nets about $7,962/month (6.7% margin), breaks even near 71.1% occupancy, turns profitable around month 13 and needs about $200,878 cash. The 100-client PASSPORT-only model nets about $2,840/month (1.8%), breaks even near 83.9% occupancy, turns profitable around month 19 and needs about $398,450. PASSPORT hours (60/month) are an operator estimate. Do not assume referral volume.

checklist.task: Understand PASSPORT slot limits and demand signals
checklist.instructions: PASSPORT enrollment requires an open slot that does not exceed the CMS-authorized limit. ODA data show ending caseload of 21,190 in Nov 2025 and 18,074 in June 2026; the Aug 2026 figure (13,196) looked inconsistent and is not relied on. Contracted PASSPORT providers rose from 3,565 (Jul 2025) to 4,115 (Aug 2026). Competition for referrals is rising.

checklist.task: Learn the participant-directed and Ohio Home Care Waiver options
checklist.instructions: Under PASSPORT participant direction, the individual is the employer and the provider is the employee. The Ohio Home Care Waiver serves people from birth through age 59 (secondary source). The home care attendant rate (S5125) includes personal care tasks in the unit rate. Decide which pathway, if any, fits your business.

checklist.task: Prepare for Electronic Visit Verification (EVV)
checklist.instructions: EVV requires direct care workers who provide certain personal care and home health services to electronically report six items: service type, recipient, date, location, worker, and start/end time. Ohio's state-provided Sandata system and devices are free to providers. An alternate EVV vendor would be at your cost, and ODM paused alternate-vendor applications on May 13, 2026. T1019 (personal care aide) is on the ODM EVV service code list.

checklist.task: Watch pending EVV rule changes under Senate Bill 315
checklist.instructions: ODM has said it will file rules requiring GPS for all EVV providers and begin rulemaking to require live-in caregivers to use EVV as a condition of payment. The Ohio Auditor of State reported that Ohio had not yet required EVV as a condition of payment and that ODM was phasing it in. Final status was not verified. Check the ODM EVV page quarterly.

checklist.task: Prepare for increased Medicaid program-integrity scrutiny
checklist.instructions: ODM announced a June 2026 payment suspension for 49 high-risk home health providers showing potential fraud red flags. Keep complete time, EVV, supervision and screening records. Hold extra cash in reserve if you bill Medicaid, since payment suspensions and slow payment can strain cash flow.

checklist.task: Confirm the PASSPORT billing portal and invoicing process
checklist.instructions: ODA is moving certified PASSPORT providers to the S-AGE provider portal for referrals and invoices in Q1 2026 (secondary source). Get portal access and training from your Area Agency on Aging once certified.

checklist.task: Check the October 1, 2026 prior-authorization notice for state plan home health
checklist.instructions: A secondary notice says state plan home health fee-for-service claims require prior authorization beginning October 1, 2026, with a grace period for waiver recipients. An official ODM notice was not retrieved. Confirm with ODM before relying on it, and note that it concerns home health, not private-pay nonmedical care.

checklist.task: File the ODH license renewal at least 90 days before expiration
checklist.instructions: A renewal is timely only if filed at least 90 days before the license expires. The renewal fee is $250 (about $6.94/month amortized in the model). Re-check the current fee and form in OAC 3701-60-03 and on the ODH page. Keep the bond active throughout.

checklist.task: Keep the $20,000 surety bond continuously in force
checklist.instructions: Pay the bond premium annually and confirm with the surety that the bond stays active. Send ODH any replacement bond information within the 10-day change-notice window if the surety or terms change.

checklist.task: Send ODH written notice of changes within 10 days
checklist.instructions: Changes in ownership, address, contact details or other application information require written notice to ODH within ten days. Keep a copy and proof of delivery.

checklist.task: Run a monthly screening and credential audit
checklist.instructions: Confirm every direct-care employee still passes the ORC 3740.11 screening. Review training logs (six hours of annual in-service for Medicaid aides), time records and incident reports. Fix gaps within the month.

checklist.task: Review wages each January against the Ohio minimum wage and local market
checklist.instructions: Ohio's minimum wage was $11.00 in 2026 and can change each January. Re-check the Department of Commerce notice and your pay scale. The model's $16.57 aide wage is a median; if you must pay more to recruit, re-run your margin, since each extra $1/hour of aide pay on 83.2 hours per client adds about $83 per client per month before burden.

checklist.task: Review insurance, BWC and unemployment rates each year
checklist.instructions: Re-quote liability and bond coverage annually. Review your BWC class and experience rating and your ODJFS unemployment rate when notices arrive. Update the model's payroll burden assumptions with actual figures.

checklist.task: Monitor Ohio rule and rate changes
checklist.instructions: Check quarterly: OAC Chapter 3701-60 (next scheduled review 01/27/2028), ODM Schedules and Rates, ODA rate sheets, ODM EVV and program-integrity pages, and the status of the Medicaid enrollment moratorium that runs to November 14, 2026.
